title: The Village That Shared One Heart
summary: In Everfeel, everyone feels what everyone else feels — no one is ever alone in a sorrow or a joy. But Mira discovers that a village that shares every feeling can never let anyone feel a hard thing all the way through, and learns that some feelings have to be felt alone before they can be shared.

chapters.title: Where No One Feels Alone
chapters.body:
In the village of Everfeel, no one ever felt anything alone.

It was the village's ancient blessing, and every soul born there shared in it: they all felt what each other felt. When one villager was joyful, the joy spread through all of them, and the whole village glowed with it. When one was sad, everyone felt the sadness, and gathered close, and shared the weight. No one in Everfeel ever suffered a grief by themselves, or celebrated a happiness alone. Every feeling was a shared feeling, flowing between all of them like water between connected pools, so that a single person's heart was really everyone's heart, and everyone's heart was one.

To outsiders, it sounded like paradise. And in many ways it was. There was a deep, warm togetherness in Everfeel that other villages never knew. No one was ever lonely. No one ever cried alone in the dark. When your heart broke, a hundred hearts broke with you and held you up; when your heart soared, a hundred hearts soared alongside. The people of Everfeel loved their shared heart, and pitied the cold isolated folk of other places, who had to feel their feelings all by themselves.

Mira was thirteen, and she had grown up in the warm shared heart of Everfeel, and had never questioned it — until the winter her grandmother died.

Her grandmother had been the person Mira loved most in all the world, and when she died, Mira felt her grief rise up enormous and terrible — and then felt it immediately spread out through the whole village, shared, divided, softened, as everyone in Everfeel felt it with her and took a portion of the weight. And that was supposed to be the blessing. That was supposed to help. But Mira felt something strange and troubling: the moment her grief spread out and was shared, it stopped being fully hers. It got... managed. Smoothed. A hundred people feeling a portion of her grief meant no one, including Mira, ever felt the whole terrible depth of it. The village absorbed it, dispersed it, comforted it away — and Mira was left feeling that she had never quite been allowed to grieve her grandmother all the way down, because the shared heart had caught the grief and spread it thin before she could feel the full weight of it herself.

And she noticed something else, in the days after. Because everyone shared her grief, everyone wanted it to ease — naturally, for it was their grief too, and they didn't want to hurt. So the village, without meaning any unkindness, gently pushed Mira's grief toward healing faster than she was ready. They shared it, and soothed it, and moved it along, because a feeling that everyone feels is a feeling everyone wants over with. And Mira found she couldn't stay in her grief long enough to truly feel it, to sit with it, to let it teach her what grief teaches — because the shared heart kept smoothing it away for the comfort of all.

She began to wonder, for the first time in her life, whether there were some feelings that a person needed to feel alone — all the way through, at their full terrible depth — before they could be shared. And wondering that, in the village of the shared heart, felt almost like a betrayal.

chapters.title: The Feeling That Couldn't Be Shared
chapters.body:
Mira went to the oldest woman in Everfeel — the keeper of the village's old knowledge — and told her the troubling thing she'd felt: that the shared heart had not let her grieve her grandmother fully, that her deepest grief had been smoothed away before she could feel it all the way down.

And the old woman, to Mira's surprise, nodded slowly, with a sad understanding.

"You've felt it, then," she said. "The thing most people here never let themselves notice. The shared heart is a blessing, child — truly. No one lonely, no one unsupported, every joy multiplied and every sorrow divided. But it has a cost, and the cost is this: some feelings can only do their work if you feel them alone, all the way through, at their full depth. And the shared heart never lets you. It catches every deep feeling and spreads it thin before it can finish."

"But why would anyone want to feel a grief alone?" Mira asked. "At its full depth? That sounds terrible."

"It is terrible," the old woman agreed. "But it's also necessary. Think about what a deep grief does, child, when you're allowed to feel it fully. It hollows you out — and in the hollow, it makes room. It teaches you how deep your love went, by showing you how deep the loss goes. It changes you, slowly, into someone who has been all the way to the bottom of a sorrow and climbed back up — and that person is deeper, and wiser, and more able to truly understand another's pain, because they've known their own all the way down. A grief felt fully, alone, is how a shallow person becomes a deep one. But a grief that's shared before it's felt — spread thin, smoothed away, managed by a hundred kind hearts — never does that work. It's comforted away before it can hollow you out and remake you. And so the people of Everfeel, for all our warmth, stay a little shallow. We never feel anything all the way to the bottom. We catch each other's feelings before they can finish."

Mira thought about this, and understood that it was true. The people of Everfeel were warm, and kind, and never lonely — but there was a way in which none of them was very deep. No one had ever been all the way to the bottom of a feeling, because the shared heart always caught them partway down. They comforted, but they didn't quite understand, because true understanding comes from having felt a thing fully yourself, and no one in Everfeel ever had.

"There's an old way," the old woman said quietly, "to step outside the shared heart. For a time. To close yourself off from it, and feel a feeling alone, all the way through, before opening yourself back up to share it. It's painful — you'd feel your grief at its full depth, with no one to divide it, truly alone in it for the first time in your life. But it's the only way to feel a thing all the way to the bottom. And a person who's done that — who's felt one feeling fully, alone, and come back — is the only kind of person who can truly share feelings afterward, instead of just spreading them thin. Would you do that, child? Feel your grandmother's loss alone, all the way down, terrible as it would be?"

And Mira, aching to grieve her grandmother truly, and frightened of what it would mean to feel it all alone, had to decide.

chapters.title: Felt All the Way Down
chapters.body:
Mira chose to do it. She used the old way the wise woman taught her, and she closed herself off from the shared heart of Everfeel — for the first time in her life, alone inside her own feelings — and she let herself grieve her grandmother all the way down.

And it was terrible, exactly as the old woman had promised. Without the village to divide it, Mira's grief came upon her at its full, undiluted depth, and it was enormous, and it was crushing, and she was utterly alone in it. She wept as she had never wept, because no one was taking a portion of the weight; she felt the whole of it, the entire measure of her love turned to loss, with nothing to soften or smooth or spread it. It hollowed her out. She went all the way to the bottom of the sorrow, the dark cold bottom that the shared heart had never let her reach, and she stayed there, alone, and felt it completely.

And something happened at the bottom that could never have happened in the shared shallows. Down there, alone in the full depth of her grief, Mira understood — really understood, in her hollowed-out heart — how much her grandmother had meant, exactly how deep the love had run, precisely what had been lost. The full depth of the grief showed her the full depth of the love, and that knowledge remade her. She was not the same girl at the bottom of that sorrow that she'd been at the top. She was deeper. She had been all the way down, alone, and she was learning the shape of the climb back up.

And when, in time, she did climb back up — when she had felt the grief all the way through, and it had done its slow hollowing work, and begun at last to ease on its own — Mira opened herself back up to the shared heart of Everfeel. And now something was different. Now, when she shared her feelings with the village, she wasn't just spreading a feeling thin before it could finish. She was sharing a feeling she had already felt all the way to the bottom — a deep thing, a whole thing, a feeling that had remade her. And the villagers, feeling it, felt something they'd rarely felt: the true depth of a grief fully known, and the hard-won peace on the other side of it. Mira had brought something back from the bottom that she could only have gotten by going there alone.

And Mira understood, at last, the thing that made the shared heart truly work. The blessing of Everfeel was never meant to spare people from feeling their deepest feelings alone. It was meant to receive those feelings after they'd been fully felt — to share the depth, not to prevent it. A feeling shared before it's felt is spread thin and smoothed away, and no one grows. But a feeling felt fully, alone, all the way to the bottom, and then shared — that is the true blessing. That is how a whole village of people can be both deep and together: each person feels their hardest feelings all the way through, alone, and is remade by them, and then brings that depth back to share, so that the shared heart is a heart of deep people who have each been to their own bottom, rather than shallow people who never let each other finish.

Mira taught this to Everfeel — gently, over years, for it was a hard truth for a village that loved its warmth. She taught them that there is a time to close yourself off and feel a thing alone, all the way down, and a time to open back up and share it. That the two are not enemies, but partners. That you cannot truly share a feeling you have never fully felt, and you cannot fully feel the deepest feelings while a hundred kind hearts are smoothing them away. And she taught them that solitude — real aloneness, inside your own feelings, all the way to the bottom — is not the opposite of togetherness, but its foundation: for only people who have been alone with their own depths have any real depth to bring back and share.

Everfeel changed, slowly. It was still the warm village of the shared heart, where no one was ever truly lonely. But now the people understood that sometimes a person needed to step away, into their own solitude, to feel a hard thing all the way through — and instead of rushing to share and smooth and soften it, they learned to let each other go to the bottom alone, and to wait, and to welcome each other back when the feeling had been fully felt. And the shared heart of Everfeel became something deeper than it had ever been: not a way to avoid ever feeling alone, but a way to bring the hard-won depths of solitude back into the warmth of togetherness — so that the village felt everything, at last, all the way down, and shared it, all the way across.
